name: Snort
oracle_text:
Each player may discard their hand and draw five cards. Then Snort deals 5 damage to each opponent who discarded their hand this way.
Flashback {5}{R} (You may cast this card from your graveyard for its flashback cost. Then exile it.)
blocked_sentences: Each player may discard their hand and draw five cards. Then Snort deals 5 damage to each opponent who discarded their hand this way.

needs.what: A way for a `may` that is resolved once per player (inside `for_each_player`) to record which players accepted, plus a player spec that later selects exactly that recorded set -- so a *subsequent* effect in the same resolution can say "each opponent who did this this way". Concretely: something like an `as` binding on `may` that accumulates the accepting player ids across the loop, readable afterwards as `{"players": {"binding": "accepted"}}` on `damage`. The first half of the sentence ("Each player may discard their hand and draw five cards") is already expressible as `for_each_player` over `each_player` wrapping a `may` whose `player` is `{"binding": "each_player"}` with `discard` + `draw`; only the back-reference is blocked.
needs.why_existing_wont_do: `set_flag`/`has_flag` is the closest recording mechanism and is object-scoped, not player-scoped: `op_set_flag` writes into `obj.flags` of battlefield objects only, and the `has_flag` condition is always asked of `ctx.source_oid`, the ability's own source -- so it cannot say anything about a player. `set_turn_flag`/`has_turn_flag` is the same shape keyed by oid. `for_each_player` does bind `each_player`, but the binding is overwritten on every iteration and restored at the end of the loop, so nothing survives to be read after the loop. `join_forces` is the only op that accumulates across a player loop and it accumulates an integer total, not the set of seats that said yes. Folding the `damage` into the `may`'s own `effects` is the tempting near miss and is wrong in two visible ways: it damages each opponent before the next opponent has been asked (in multiplayer a player can be killed mid-loop, changing later choices), and it splits one simultaneous damage event into several separate ones, which is observable to damage triggers and to prevention shields.
